area-1.name: Reporting processes
area-1.ARO1.hint:
When a security vulnerability is found and fixed in your product, it’s important to inform users in a clear, responsible, and secure way. You should have a formal vulnerability disclosure policy that describes how and when you publish information about vulnerabilities and security updates. A good security advisory includes all the information users need to understand the issue and take action: what the vulnerability is, which products and versions are affected, how severe the issue is, and what steps users need to take to stay secure. This may include installing a patch, changing a setting, or disabling a feature temporarily.

To ensure that users trust the information, you should protect the authenticity of the advisory—using digital signatures, secure websites, or other methods that confirm the message really comes from you and hasn’t been tampered with. Sometimes, it might be safer to delay publishing technical details of a fixed vulnerability—for example, if users haven’t had time to update and attackers could exploit the information. When you do this, it’s important to clearly document why the decision was made, showing that it was done to protect users and not to hide problems.

Once an advisory is published, it should explain how users can check if their specific product is affected and exactly what to do. This includes clear instructions written in accessible language, with links to any necessary updates or tools. Ultimately, transparency and trust are key—users must be able to understand, verify, and act on the information you provide to keep their systems safe.
area-1.ARO1.questions.Q1.text: Is there a formal process for publishing vulnerability advisories that includes clear, accessible remediation guidance for users?
area-1.ARO1.questions.Q2.text: When publishing a security advisory, do you include information about the vulnerability, affected products, severity, and remediation steps?
area-1.ARO1.questions.Q3.text: How do you ensure the authenticity of the advisory, for example through digital signatures or other validation methods?
area-1.ARO1.questions.Q4.text: Are there situations where you choose to delay sharing details about a fixed vulnerability because it might be safer for users?
area-1.ARO1.questions.Q5.text: When that happens, do you clearly document why the decision was made and how it was justified?
area-1.ARO1.questions.Q6.text: When you publish a security advisory, does it clearly explain how users can check if their product is affected and what steps they should take to stay protected?
area-1.ARO2.hint:
Coordinated Vulnerability Disclosure (CVD) is about working constructively with people who report security issues in your product—whether they are researchers, customers, or other external stakeholders. You should have a public vulnerability disclosure policy that shows your openness to receiving reports and explains how reporters can contact you. This policy should clearly state that you will handle reports respectfully, investigate them seriously, and keep the reporter informed.

When someone submits a potential vulnerability, you should acknowledge their report within 7 days, confirming that you've received it. Then, as you investigate the issue, you should stay in contact with the reporter—letting them know whether the vulnerability is confirmed, what your remediation plans are, and when (or if) you plan to publish an advisory. This open line of communication builds trust and often leads to better-quality reports.

It’s important to have a documented internal process for how you manage CVD: how submissions are tracked, how teams are involved in analysis and mitigation, and how decisions are made about publication timing. If a vulnerability is valid, you should also make sure the reporter is informed before disclosure, and ideally involved in reviewing the advisory.

Even if you’re a small company, it’s possible to handle CVD well—by setting up a dedicated contact point (like an email or web form), using templates to track cases, and being clear and timely in your responses. Good vulnerability disclosure practices not only help improve product security but also demonstrate your credibility and responsibility to customers and regulators.
area-1.ARO2.questions.Q1.text: Do you have a public vulnerability disclosure policy that includes your commitment to Coordinated Vulnerability Disclosure? - Point 8 of paragraph 13  is excluded from the obligations of the authorized representative.
area-1.ARO2.questions.Q2.text: Is there a documented process for engaging with external stakeholders (e.g., reporters, coordinators) during the vulnerability handling lifecycle?
area-1.ARO2.questions.Q3.text: Are reporters acknowledged within 7 calendar days of submission, and are they informed of investigation results and publication plans?
area-1.ARO2.questions.Q4.text: When someone reports a potential vulnerability, do you get back to them within 7 days to confirm you’ve received it?
area-1.ARO2.questions.Q5.text: How do you keep the reporter informed throughout the investigation, including whether and when the vulnerability details will be disclosed?
area-1.ARO3.requirement: Processing and monitoring of vulnerability reporting
area-1.ARO3.hint:
It’s essential to provide a secure, reliable, and easy-to-find way for people outside your organization—such as customers, security researchers, or partners—to report vulnerabilities in your product. This is not only a best practice but also a requirement under the CRA. At minimum, a clear contact method shall be specified and available, like a dedicated email address (preferably with encryption support, such as PGP) or a secure web form. This contact information should be prominently published on a website or in the documentation.

 You should ensure that a communication channel regarding the vulnerability is established with the manufacturer. This is especially important if you maintain a single point of contact for product users, so you can also stay up-to-date on the progress of any vulnerabilities they report.
 
You should keep the reporter and any other relevant stakeholders informed. Let them know you’ve received the report, whether the issue is valid, and when it is expected to fix or disclose it.
 
If you're using public reporting channels, make sure they are tested regularly and clearly explained to users so they know how to reach out if they discover a problem.
area-1.ARO3.questions.Q1.text: Is there a secure and reliable mechanism in place for people outside your organization to report a vulnerability? For example: an encrypted email address or a protected web form?
area-1.ARO3.questions.Q2.text: Do you regularly monitor your reporting channels to make sure new vulnerability reports are seen and handled quickly?
area-1.ARO3.questions.Q3.text: Does the general reporting of vulnerabilities include such data as vulnerable product, general nature of the exploit and vulnerability, corrective or mitigationg measures?
area-1.ARO3.questions.Q4.text: How do you track and manage incoming vulnerability reports—do you assign them a unique ID or reference to follow their progress?
area-1.ARO3.questions.Q5.text: How do you keep relevant stakeholders—such as the reporter or impacted partners—informed during the investigation and resolution of a vulnerability?
area-1.ARO3.questions.Q6.text: What is the mechanism available for users to report vulnerabilities or reach out for support. For instance, do you provide a clear and accessible contact method like an email address or web form?
area-1.ARO4.hint:
Incident reporting is a critical part of your cybersecurity responsibilities under the CRA. You should have a formal incident management policy that outlines how your organization identifies, records, classifies, and reports security incidents. This policy should clearly define what qualifies as a “security incident” and establish who is responsible for classifying its severity—usually someone from your security, engineering, or compliance team.

To manage incidents effectively, you need an internal system to record each event—this can be a ticketing system, an internal log, or a specialized incident tracking platform. It’s important that your team uses this system consistently to document what happened, when, what the impact was, and what steps were taken in response.

For incidents that are severe—those that affect the confidentiality, integrity, or availability of your product or introduce significant cybersecurity risks—you are legally required to send an early warning notification within 24 hours of becoming aware of the issue, and a full notification within 72 hours. You should define clear criteria in your policy for what qualifies as “severe,” based on risk to users, exploitability, or the scope of the impact.

To meet the CRA’s deadlines, you need to ensure you have a well-practiced process and that the responsible people know what to do when a severe incident occurs. The report must be submitted to the CSIRT designated as coordinator, using the electronic notification end-point set up for this purpose via the ENISA-managed single reporting platform. If your organization is not based in the EU, you must still follow these rules and submit to the appropriate CSIRT based on where your representative, importer, or largest user base is located.

Timely, accurate reporting is not only a legal obligation—it also helps protect your users, limit reputational damage, and support a broader EU-wide response to cybersecurity threats.
area-1.ARO4.questions.Q1.text: Is there an internal incident management process?
area-1.ARO4.questions.Q2.text: What mechanisms are implemented internally for recording incidents?
area-1.ARO4.questions.Q3.text: Who is responsible for the classification of a given security incident?
area-1.ARO4.questions.Q4.text: What are the set criteria for classifying an incident as severe?
area-1.ARO4.questions.Q5.text: How do you ensure that an early warning notification of a severe incident having an impact on the security of the product with digital elements, without undue delay and in any event within 24 hours of the manufacturer becoming aware of it?
area-1.ARO4.questions.Q6.text: How do you ensure that all severe incidents are notified without undue delay and in any event within 72 hours?
area-1.ARO4.questions.Q7.text: What is the reporting channel for incidents toward the notified CSIRT ?
area-2.name: Internal documents of the organization (policies and procedures)
area-2.ARO5.hint:
A single point of contact is a designated person or team responsible for handling all cybersecurity-related communications about your product. This contact should be easy for users and authorities to find and reach out to, ensuring clear and timely communication about vulnerabilities, security incidents, or other important issues. Having a reliable single point of contact helps coordinate responses efficiently and builds trust with customers and regulators by showing that your organization takes cybersecurity seriously and is prepared to act when needed.
Additionally, you should clearly indicate the availability of a single point of contact and ensure that this information is kept up to date.
area-2.ARO5.questions.Q1.text: Do you have a clearly designated single point of contact for cybersecurity issues related to your product?
area-2.ARO5.questions.Q2.text: Is the contact information for this single point of contact readily accessible to users and market surveillance authorities?
area-2.ARO6.hint:
You should consider and include in your procedures the situation, when you found an actively exploited vulnerability in the product, incident having an impact on the security of the product. 
The process, procedures of reporting to the relevant CSIRT and to ENISA within required timeframes shall be provided: 
- within 24h - early warning, 
- within 72h - general information report , 
- within 14 days - a final report on actively exploited vulnerability,
- within a month - a final report on any severe incident.
area-2.ARO6.questions.Q1.text: Does the organization have a defined process and procedures for reporting to a CSIRT and ENISA actively exploited vulnerabilities and serious security incidents of the product?
area-2.ARO6.questions.Q2.text: Does the process, documentation include early warning about the actively exploited vulnerability to be sent within 24 hours of discovery to the relevant CSIRT and/or ENISA?
area-2.ARO6.questions.Q3.text: Does the process, documentation provide a description of process for detailed vulnerability reports submition within 72 hours of discovery, via the reporting platform, to the relevant CSIRT and/or ENISA?
area-2.ARO6.questions.Q4.text: Does the organization have a defined process process for a vulnerability final report submition within 14 days of the corrective measure being implemented?
area-2.ARO6.questions.Q6.text: Does the organization have a defined process for an incident final report submition within one month of the corrective measure being implemented?
area-2.ARO6.questions.Q8.text: Does the process ensure that information about exploited vulnerabilities or severe incidents impacting the product (if any are found) is provided in a machine-readable format suitable for automatic processing?
area-2.ARO7.requirement: Copy of the EU declaration of conformity
area-2.ARO7.hint:
The technical documentation drawn up before the products are placed on the market, shall be continuously updated, at least during the support period. 
You shall keep the technical documentation and the EU declaration of conformity available for the market surveillance authorities for at least 10 years after the product has been placed on the market or for the support period, whichever is longer.
area-2.ARO7.questions.Q1.text: Are the technical documentation and correspondence relating to any conformity assessment procedure drawn up in an official language of the Member State in which the notified body is established or in a language acceptable to that body?
area-2.ARO7.questions.Q2.text: How is the process of keeping the technical documentation and the EU declaration of conformity at the disposal of the market surveillance authorities organized?
